extracted.intended_audience: Small businesses and research partners preparing SBIR/STTR proposals to U.S. federal agencies (SBA/NIH/NSF/DOE/DOD/NASA)
extracted.subtask_description: Review criteria and program-specific requirements used by U.S. federal SBIR/STTR programs to evaluate Phase I/II proposals, including innovation, technical merit, commercialization, and eligibility/partnership rules. Covers universal criteria and agency-specific emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small business qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Small business qualification — agencies make awards based on small business qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility is a fundamental criterion for award decisions. For SBIR the small business must perform the primary work; for STTR a formal partnership with a research institution is required (see STTR partnership requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation / The Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree/Quality of the proposed innovation — 'The Innovation: Quality of the proposed innovation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers assess how novel the idea or technology is and whether it advances the state of the art. Innovation is a universal review criterion used across agencies and a key factor in Phase I evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical merit / Technical Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical merit and approach — 'Technical Approach: Methods and feasibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment focuses on the rigor, appropriateness, and feasibility of the proposed methods. For Phase I, reviewers determine scientific and technical merit and feasibility; Phase I is a 6–12 month concept phase to explore technical merit/feasibility. Typical Phase I award sizes vary by agency ($50K–$300K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial potential / Commercial Potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial potential — 'Commercial Potential: Market opportunity and competitive landscape.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators judge market opportunity, competitive positioning, and the plausibility of a path to commercialization. Commercial potential is a universal criterion and a decisive factor for Phase II selection (results of Phase I, scientific/technical merit, and commercial potential determine Phase II funding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Future market potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Future market potential — listed as a distinct universal consideration for award decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers consider longer-term market growth, scalability, and sustainability of the product or service beyond immediate commercial opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team / Qualifications
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of investigators and key personnel for relevant expertise, track record, and access to necessary facilities or infrastructure to carry out the project successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer Discovery / Evidence of market need
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers look for evidence of customer engagement, validation of demand, and market discovery activities. NSF emphasizes customer discovery heavily; agencies may weight customer discovery differently when scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase I evaluation focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase I awards determine scientific and technical merit and feasibility of ideas that appear to have commercial potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phase I is a concept phase (6–12 months) supporting exploration of technical merit or feasibility. Typical awards vary by agency ($50K–$300K). Evaluation emphasizes feasibility and proof-of-concept over full commercialization readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase II commercialization plan requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A succinct commercialization plan must be included with each Phase II proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commercialization plan is a mandatory component of Phase II submissions. At NIH the commercialization plan is weighted as heavily as the research plan; at NSF it is weighted even more prominently. Typical Phase II awards range from $750K–$2M depending on agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase III commercialization/procurement expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase III — No SBIR funding; intended to use non-SBIR funds to commercialize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phase III is expected to be funded from private-sector or non-SBIR federal sources. The government may issue contracts for products/services derived from SBIR work and can sole-source from SBIR Phase III companies; reviewers and applicants should consider downstream procurement/commercialization paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: STTR partnership and work allocation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: STTR requires partnership with a research institution (≥30% of work performed by partner); SBIR requires the small business perform the primary work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility and work allocation are enforceable program rules and also affect evaluations (responsibility, capacity, and institutional support). For STTR, at least 30% of the work must be performed by the research partner.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH-specific emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH: Health-related innovations, similar to R01 review with commercialization addendum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH reviews SBIR/STTR applications using criteria similar to R01 (scientific rigor, significance, investigators, innovation, approach, environment) but places explicit weight on commercialization via an added commercialization component; NIH weights commercialization as heavily as the research plan for Phase II.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF-specific emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF: Broader STEM focus, heavy weight on customer discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSF places particular emphasis on customer discovery and commercialization readiness; the commercialization plan may be weighted more prominently at NSF than at other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE-specific emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE: Energy/environmental focus; topics released annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should align proposals with DOE topic areas and priorities for energy and environmental technologies; topic announcements and priorities are updated on an annual cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOD-specific emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: DOD: Defense applications; topics released three times per year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOD SBIR/STTR topics target defense-relevant applications; solicitations are issued multiple times per year (three releases), and proposers should align with current DOD topics and needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: NASA-specific emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: NASA: Aerospace technology; topics aligned with mission directorates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should align with NASA mission directorates and aerospace technology priorities; topic alignment with mission needs is a significant evaluative factor.
